docs.title: Reading and writing
docs.text:
HiReS reads and writes YOLO segmentation label files and exports measurements as tables. The examples on this page create their own small files, so they can be run as they are.

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> import hires

docs.title: The label format
docs.text:
A label file is a plain-text file with one object per line:

class_id x1 y1 x2 y2 ... xn yn [confidence]
class_id Integer class label. x1 y1 ... xn yn The polygon vertices in normalized coordinates: x as a fraction of the image width, y as a fraction of the image height. At least three points are required. The polygon is closed implicitly. confidence Optional detection score in [0, 1]. Every vertex contributes two numbers, so a trailing value that makes the count odd is the confidence.

This is the format written by Ultralytics with save_txt=True, save_conf=True, and without the confidence, the format expected for training. By convention the label file of scan.tif is called scan.txt.

Here is a file with a prediction (confidence 0.87) and a ground-truth object (no confidence):

>>> Path("labels").mkdir()
>>> _ = Path("labels/scan.txt").write_text(
...     "0 0.1 0.1 0.3 0.1 0.3 0.2 0.1 0.2 0.87\n"
...     "1 0.5 0.5 0.7 0.5 0.6 0.8\n"
... )

docs.title: Reading one file
docs.text:
hires.read_txt returns a Collection named after the file:

>>> collection = hires.read_txt("labels/scan.txt")
>>> collection
Collection(name='scan', n=2)
>>> collection[0]
Annotation(class_id=0, confidence=0.870, vertices=4)
>>> collection[1]
Annotation(class_id=1, confidence=None, vertices=3)

docs.title: Telling HiReS the image size
docs.text:
Label files do not record how large the image is, and without that measurements cannot be expressed in pixels. There are two ways to supply it. If the image is at hand, pass it; only the file header is read, so this is fast even for very large scans:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import cv2
>>> Path("images").mkdir()
>>> _ = cv2.imwrite("images/scan.png", np.zeros((1000, 2000, 3), dtype=np.uint8))
>>> collection = hires.read_txt("labels/scan.txt", image="images/scan.png")
>>> collection
Collection(name='scan', n=2, image_size=(2000, 1000))
>>> collection.image_path.name
'scan.png'

Otherwise give the size directly, as (width, height):

>>> hires.read_txt("labels/scan.txt", image_size=(2000, 1000))
Collection(name='scan', n=2, image_size=(2000, 1000))

Collection.from_txt is an alias of read_txt.

docs.title: Invalid lines
docs.text:
A line may be unreadable: too few numbers, text where a number should be, a confidence outside [0, 1], or a polygon without area. The on_error argument decides what happens.

on_error Behaviour "warn" (default) Skip the line and emit one HiresWarning per file "raise" Raise AnnotationFormatError "ignore" Skip the line silently 
>>> _ = Path("broken.txt").write_text(
...     "0 0.1 0.1 0.3 0.1 0.3 0.2\n"
...     "1 0.5 0.5 oops\n"
... )
>>> hires.read_txt("broken.txt", on_error="ignore")
Collection(name='broken', n=1)
>>> hires.read_txt("broken.txt", on_error="raise")
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
hires.errors.AnnotationFormatError: broken.txt:2: expected a class id and at least 3 points

docs.title: Polygon repair
docs.text:
Self-intersecting outlines, such as a "bow tie", are common in model output. They are repaired on reading; if the repair splits the outline into several parts, the largest part is kept:

>>> _ = Path("bowtie.txt").write_text("0 0.0 0.0 0.4 0.4 0.4 0.0 0.0 0.2\n")
>>> repaired = hires.read_txt("bowtie.txt")[0]
>>> repaired.polygon.is_valid
True
>>> round(repaired.polygon.area, 4)
0.0533

docs.title: Reading a directory
docs.text:
hires.read_album reads every *.txt file of a directory, sorted by name, into an Album named after the directory:

>>> _ = Path("labels/scan_2.txt").write_text("0 0.2 0.2 0.4 0.2 0.4 0.6 0.2 0.6\n")
>>> album = hires.read_album("labels")
>>> album
Album(name='labels', collections=2, annotations=3)
>>> album.names
['scan', 'scan_2']
>>> album["scan_2"]
Collection(name='scan_2', n=1)

With image_dir, each {stem}.txt is bound to the image {image_dir}/{stem} with the extension .tif, .tiff, .png, .jpg or .jpeg, tried in that order. Label files without a matching image are still loaded, just without an image size:

>>> album = hires.read_album("labels", image_dir="images")
>>> album["scan"].image_size
(2000, 1000)
>>> album["scan_2"].image_size is None
True

An explicit list of files works too:

>>> hires.read_album(["labels/scan.txt", "bowtie.txt"], name="selection")
Album(name='selection', collections=2, annotations=3)

Album.from_dir is an alias of read_album.

docs.title: Reading class names
docs.text:
Label files contain only class ids. The names live in the dataset data.yaml, or inside the model weights:

>>> _ = Path("data.yaml").write_text("names:\n  0: d_pulex\n  1: d_galeata\n")
>>> hires.read_class_names("data.yaml")
{0: 'd_pulex', 1: 'd_galeata'}
>>> hires.read_class_names("DaphnAI.pt")  # doctest: +SKIP

Reading names from weights needs the yolo extra. The resulting {class_id: label} dict is what the plotting and evaluation functions accept as class_names=.

docs.title: Exporting measurements
docs.text:
to_frame returns one row per annotation:

>>> frame = collection.to_frame()
>>> list(frame.columns[:8])
['name', 'image_path', 'image_width', 'image_height', 'dpi', 'unit', 'class_id', 'confidence']
>>> frame[["class_id", "confidence", "area", "perimeter", "circularity"]]
   class_id  confidence     area  perimeter  circularity
0         0        0.87  40000.0  1000.0000       0.5027
1         1         NaN  60000.0  1121.1103       0.5999
Column Content name Collection name image_path Path of the image, if known image_width, image_height Image size in pixels, if known dpi, unit Physical scale, if set class_id Class label confidence Detection score, empty for ground truth area … obb_length The nine traits in hires.TRAIT_NAMES

The units of the trait columns depend on what the collection knows (see Units):

The collection has Lengths in Areas in no image_size normalized units (with a warning) normalized units² image_size pixels pixels² image_size, dpi and unit unit unit²

to_csv writes the same table to a file, and to_records returns it as a list of dicts:

>>> collection.to_csv("scan_shapes.csv")
>>> len(Path("scan_shapes.csv").read_text().splitlines())   # header + 2 rows
3
>>> collection.to_records()[1]["area"]
60000.0

The album methods of the same name concatenate all collections and add a leading album column. To measure the whole album in pixels, every collection needs its image, so we first add the one that was missing:

>>> _ = cv2.imwrite("images/scan_2.png", np.zeros((500, 500, 3), dtype=np.uint8))
>>> album = hires.read_album("labels", image_dir="images")
>>> album.to_frame()[["album", "name", "class_id", "area"]]
    album    name  class_id     area
0  labels    scan         0  40000.0
1  labels    scan         1  60000.0
2  labels  scan_2         0  20000.0

summary gives one row per collection:

>>> album.summary()[["name", "n_annotations", "image_width", "image_height"]]
     name  n_annotations  image_width  image_height
0    scan              2         2000          1000
1  scan_2              1          500           500

docs.title: Writing label files
docs.text:
>>> collection.to_txt("out/scan.txt")
>>> print(Path("out/scan.txt").read_text())
0 0.100000 0.100000 0.300000 0.100000 0.300000 0.200000 0.100000 0.200000 0.870000
1 0.500000 0.500000 0.700000 0.500000 0.600000 0.800000

Coordinates are written with six decimals. With confidence=False the confidence is left out, which turns predictions into training labels:

>>> collection.to_txt("out/scan_training.txt", confidence=False)
>>> print(Path("out/scan_training.txt").read_text())
0 0.100000 0.100000 0.300000 0.100000 0.300000 0.200000 0.100000 0.200000
1 0.500000 0.500000 0.700000 0.500000 0.600000 0.800000

An album writes one {name}.txt per collection into a directory:

>>> written = album.to_txt("out/album")
>>> sorted(path.name for path in written)
['scan.txt', 'scan_2.txt']

Only polygon exteriors are written; the format cannot represent holes.

docs.title: Saving crops
docs.text:
save_crops writes one image per annotation, cropped to its bounding box. The collection must know its image:

>>> crops = collection.save_crops("crops", padding=10)
>>> [path.name for path in crops]
['scan_0000_class_0.png', 'scan_0001_class_1.png']
>>> cv2.imread(str(crops[0])).shape
(120, 420, 3)

Files are named {prefix}_{index:04d}_class_{class_id}.png, where the prefix defaults to the collection name. Pixels outside the polygon are blacked out unless mask=False. Album.save_crops writes one sub-directory per collection.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
The low-level helpers in hires.io are public:

>>> [path.name for path in hires.io.find_images("images")]
['scan.png', 'scan_2.png']
>>> hires.io.read_image_size("images/scan.png")
(2000, 1000)
>>> hires.io.read_image("images/scan.png").shape
(1000, 2000, 3)

Three conventions are worth knowing:

  • Sizes are (width, height); array shapes are (height, width, channels), as in NumPy.
  • Images are read as 8-bit BGR arrays, the OpenCV convention. Functions in hires.plot return RGB arrays, ready for Matplotlib.
  • EXIF orientation is ignored. Pixel coordinates always refer to the stored raster, so that labels, image sizes and pixels agree.

docs.text:

  • The data model

docs.title: Morphometric traits
docs.text:
HiReS derives nine geometric descriptors from the polygon outline of every object. They correspond to the size and shape traits commonly used in ecological image analysis. Their names are listed, in order, in hires.TRAIT_NAMES.

Trait Symbol Definition Range Unit Describes area \(A\) Enclosed area \(> 0\) length² Two-dimensional size perimeter \(P\) Boundary length \(> 0\) length Size and outline complexity solidity \(S\) \(A / A_\text{hull}\) \((0, 1]\) — Depth of concavities convexity \(K\) \(P_\text{hull} / P\) \((0, 1]\) — Smoothness of the outline circularity \(C\) \(4 \pi A / P^2\) \((0, 1]\) — Compactness bbox_width Extent along the image \(x\) axis \(> 0\) length bbox_height Extent along the image \(y\) axis \(> 0\) length obb_width \(W\) Short side of the oriented bounding box \(> 0\) length Body width obb_length \(L\) Long side of the oriented bounding box \(> 0\) length Body length

docs.title: Computing traits
docs.text:
For any Shapely polygon, hires.measure returns the traits as a dict. A 4 × 2 rectangle:

>>> from shapely.geometry import box
>>> import hires
>>> traits = hires.measure(box(0, 0, 4, 2))
>>> traits["area"], traits["perimeter"], traits["obb_length"], traits["obb_width"]
(8.0, 12.0, 4.0, 2.0)
>>> for name in hires.TRAIT_NAMES:
...     print(f"{name:12} {traits[name]:.3f}")
area         8.000
perimeter    12.000
solidity     1.000
convexity    1.000
circularity  0.698
bbox_width   4.000
bbox_height  2.000
obb_width    2.000
obb_length   4.000

The shape descriptors tell shapes apart regardless of size. Compare the rectangle with a circle and with an L-shaped polygon:

>>> from shapely.geometry import Point, Polygon
>>> shapes = {
...     "rectangle": box(0, 0, 4, 2),
...     "circle": Point(0, 0).buffer(1, quad_segs=64),
...     "L-shape": Polygon([(0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 1), (1, 1), (1, 4), (0, 4)]),
... }
>>> for label, polygon in shapes.items():
...     t = hires.measure(polygon)
...     print(f"{label:10} circularity={t['circularity']:.2f}  "
...           f"solidity={t['solidity']:.2f}  convexity={t['convexity']:.2f}")
rectangle  circularity=0.70  solidity=1.00  convexity=1.00
circle     circularity=1.00  solidity=1.00  convexity=1.00
L-shape    circularity=0.34  solidity=0.61  convexity=0.89

The circle is the most compact shape (circularity 1); the L-shape has a deep concavity, which lowers its solidity.

In practice you rarely call measure yourself. A collection measures all its annotations at once, in the right units:

>>> collection = hires.Collection(
...     [
...         hires.Annotation(0, box(0.10, 0.10, 0.30, 0.20), confidence=0.9),
...         hires.Annotation(1, box(0.50, 0.50, 0.60, 0.90), confidence=0.7),
...     ],
...     name="scan",
...     image_size=(2000, 1000),
... )
>>> collection.to_frame()[["class_id", "area", "perimeter", "obb_length", "obb_width"]]
   class_id     area  perimeter  obb_length  obb_width
0         0  40000.0     1000.0       400.0      100.0
1         1  80000.0     1200.0       400.0      200.0

and a single annotation is measured with Annotation.traits, given the image size:

>>> collection[0].traits(collection.image_size)["obb_length"]
400.0

docs.title: Area
docs.text:
The surface enclosed by the outline, computed from the vertices \((x_i, y_i)\), \(i = 1 \dots n\), with the shoelace formula:

\[ A = \frac{1}{2} \left| \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( x_i \, y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} \, y_i \right) \right|, \qquad (x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) = (x_1, y_1). \]

Area is a direct estimate of body size that uses the full geometry of the object.

docs.title: Perimeter
docs.text:
The length of the boundary, the sum of the Euclidean distances between consecutive vertices:

\[ P = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sqrt{(x_{i+1} - x_i)^2 + (y_{i+1} - y_i)^2}. \]

Perimeter reflects both size and boundary complexity. It depends on the resolution of the outline: a more finely sampled, more jagged polygon has a longer perimeter than a smooth one around the same object.

docs.title: Body length and width
docs.text:
The oriented bounding box (OBB) is the rectangle of minimum area that encloses the polygon, at whatever angle achieves that minimum. With side lengths \(l_1\) and \(l_2\),

\[ L = \max(l_1, l_2), \qquad W = \min(l_1, l_2). \]

obb_length and obb_width are independent of how the organism is oriented on the scan, which makes them the appropriate measures of body length and width.

Oriented versus axis-aligned

bbox_width and bbox_height are the extents along the image axes. They depend on the orientation of the organism: for an elongated animal lying diagonally, both overestimate its width and underestimate its length. Use them for cropping, not for morphometry.

docs.title: Circularity
docs.text:
\[ C = \frac{4 \pi A}{P^2} \]

Equal to 1 for a circle and smaller for every other shape. It decreases as an object becomes more elongated or its outline more irregular.

docs.title: Convexity
docs.text:
\[ K = \frac{P_\text{hull}}{P} \]

where \(P_\text{hull}\) is the perimeter of the convex hull. Values near 1 indicate a smooth, convex outline; lower values indicate high-frequency irregularities such as spines or a jagged boundary.

docs.title: Solidity
docs.text:
\[ S = \frac{A}{A_\text{hull}} \]

where \(A_\text{hull}\) is the area of the convex hull, the smallest convex polygon enclosing the object. Low values indicate deep concavities or appendages.

Convexity and solidity are complementary: convexity responds to roughness of the boundary, solidity to missing area.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
The traits are computed in whatever coordinate system the polygon is in. Which one that is depends on the collection:

The collection has Lengths in Areas in no image_size normalized units normalized units² image_size pixels pixels² image_size, dpi and unit unit unit²

The ratios solidity, convexity and circularity are dimensionless and do not change with scale.

Always provide the image size

In normalized coordinates a non-square image is squeezed into a square. area and solidity survive this (up to a constant factor), but every length, and with it perimeter, convexity, circularity and the bounding-box dimensions, is distorted. HiReS emits a HiresWarning when it has to measure this way. Load labels with image= or image_dir= to avoid it.

docs.title: Physical units
docs.text:
A scanner resolution in dots per inch fixes the physical size of a pixel. For a unit with \(u\) units per inch,

\[ s = \frac{u}{\text{dpi}} \]

is the edge length of one pixel. Lengths are multiplied by \(s\), areas by \(s^2\).

>>> scaled = collection.with_scale(dpi=2400, unit="um")
>>> round(scaled.pixel_size, 3)        # micrometres per pixel
10.583
>>> scaled.to_frame()[["class_id", "area", "obb_length", "obb_width"]].round(1)
   class_id       area  obb_length  obb_width
0         0  4480277.8      4233.3     1058.3
1         1  8960555.6      4233.3     2116.7

The same objects as above, now in µm² and µm. The supported units and their number per inch:

>>> hires.UNITS
{'nm': 25400000.0, 'um': 25400.0, 'mm': 25.4, 'cm': 2.54, 'm': 0.0254, 'inch': 1.0}

The keys of hires.UNITS are what unit= accepts:

unit Meaning Units per inch "nm" nanometre 25 400 000 "um" micrometre 25 400 "mm" millimetre 25.4 "cm" centimetre 2.54 "m" metre 0.0254 "inch" inch 1

dpi and unit must be given together, and the collection must know its image_size. Calling with_scale(None, None) removes the scale again.

Resolution of your images

The dpi must be the resolution at which the image was actually acquired. For a microscope, convert the calibration to dots per inch: a pixel size of \(p\) µm corresponds to \(25\,400 / p\) dpi.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text:
• A polygon with zero perimeter or zero hull area yields 0.0 for the affected ratio rather than raising.
  • If no oriented bounding box can be constructed, obb_width and obb_length are nan.
  • For polygons with holes, area excludes the holes and perimeter includes the interior boundaries. Polygons read from label files never have holes.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
HiReS was validated against manually annotated outlines of Daphnia pulex, Daphnia galeata and Simocephalus vetulus across nine full-resolution scanner images. The main findings were:

  • Automated and manual trait distributions preserved the same broad structure and relative ordering.
  • A consistent positive bias of 5–19 % was observed: a multiplicative scaling offset, not a distortion.
  • After centring by the median residual, agreement was near-perfect (\(r\) = 0.969–0.999).
  • Sample-level medians were strongly correlated (\(r\) = 0.94–0.96) despite the individual-level bias.
  • At low sampling depths (\(n\) = 10), automated medians outperformed manual subsamples in 43–62 % of cases.

The positive bias likely reflects illumination-induced halos around the organisms that are partially included in the predicted mask. To quantify the agreement on your own data, see Evaluation.

docs.title: Visualisation
docs.text:
hires.plot draws annotations, match results and evaluation charts. Two conventions hold throughout:

  • Functions that draw on an image return an RGB numpy.ndarray.
  • Functions that draw a chart return the Matplotlib Axes or Figure.

No function calls plt.show(), and every function accepts save= to write the result to a file. Every figure on this page was produced by the code shown above it.

docs.title: The example scan
docs.text:
To have something to draw, we make a small synthetic scan: a grey image with five dark blobs, two of class 0 and three of class 1. With real data, you would use the path of your scan and a collection from hires.segment or hires.read_txt.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import cv2
>>> from shapely.affinity import rotate, scale
>>> from shapely.geometry import Point
>>> import hires
>>> def blob(class_id, x, y, radius, stretch=1.0, angle=0.0):
...     outline = rotate(scale(Point(x, y).buffer(radius), yfact=stretch), angle)
...     return hires.Annotation(class_id, outline)
>>> gt = hires.Collection(
...     [
...         blob(0, 0.20, 0.25, 0.07, stretch=2.2, angle=30),
...         blob(0, 0.55, 0.30, 0.06, stretch=2.0, angle=-50),
...         blob(1, 0.70, 0.60, 0.05, stretch=1.4),
...         blob(1, 0.30, 0.70, 0.05, stretch=1.5, angle=80),
...         blob(1, 0.58, 0.78, 0.04),
...     ],
...     name="scan",
...     image_size=(600, 400),
... )
>>> scan = np.full((400, 600, 3), 200, dtype=np.uint8)
>>> for a in gt:
...     outline = np.array(a.to_pixels((600, 400)).exterior.coords, dtype=np.int32)
...     _ = cv2.fillPoly(scan, [outline], (95, 110, 120))

The "predictions" are the same outlines, grown a little, with one object missing, one given the wrong class, and one spurious detection added:

>>> def predicted(a, confidence, class_id=None):
...     return a.replace(
...         polygon=a.polygon.buffer(0.012),
...         confidence=confidence,
...         class_id=a.class_id if class_id is None else class_id,
...     )
>>> pred = hires.Collection(
...     [
...         predicted(gt[0], 0.94),
...         predicted(gt[1], 0.91),
...         predicted(gt[2], 0.83),
...         predicted(gt[3], 0.62, class_id=0),
...         blob(1, 0.75, 0.15, 0.035).replace(confidence=0.41),
...     ],
...     name="scan",
...     image_size=(600, 400),
... )
>>> names = {0: "pulex", 1: "galeata"}

docs.title: Annotations on an image
docs.text:
overlay fills each polygon in the colour of its class, draws its bounding box and writes a label index class confidence next to it:

>>> rgb = hires.plot.overlay(scan, pred, class_names=names, save="plot_overlay.png")
>>> rgb.shape, rgb.dtype
((400, 600, 3), dtype('uint8'))

The index is the position of the annotation in the collection, and for a collection read from disk, the line number in the label file. Use it to look an object up:

>>> pred[3]
Annotation(class_id=0, confidence=0.620, vertices=128)

Each element can be switched off:

>>> _ = hires.plot.overlay(
...     scan, pred, boxes=False, labels=False, alpha=0.35, save="plot_outlines.png"
... )

The first argument is either the path of an image file or an 8-bit BGR array, as returned by hires.io.read_image. Reading a large scan once and passing the array avoids decoding it again for every figure. To show the result in a notebook or a window, hand the returned array to Matplotlib:

>>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
>>> image = plt.imshow(rgb)

Colours are taken from hires.plot.PALETTE by class id and repeat after ten classes.

docs.title: Predictions versus ground truth
docs.text:
comparison colours each object by the outcome of matching:

>>> matches = hires.metrics.match(gt, pred)
>>> matches.counts()
{'tp': 3, 'misclassified': 1, 'fp': 1, 'fn': 1}
>>> _ = hires.plot.comparison(scan, matches, save="plot_comparison.png")

Colour Status Polygon drawn Green tp Prediction Orange misclassified Prediction Red fp Prediction Blue fn Missed ground truth

For the result of matching two albums, select one image first with matches.for_image(name). hires.evaluate writes this image for every scan.

docs.title: A single object
docs.text:
individual crops the image around one match and draws four panels: the ground-truth mask, the predicted mask, the raw crop, and both outlines together with the IoU and the match status.

>>> worst = matches.pick("tp", by="worst_iou")
>>> figure = hires.plot.individual(
...     worst, scan, class_names=names, figsize=(7, 7), save="plot_individual.png"
... )

When the collections were read with their images (image= or image_dir=), the image argument can be left out and is taken from the match. For many figures of one scan, read the scan once and pass the array, as here.

Close figures in loops

Matplotlib keeps every figure alive until it is closed. When producing figures in a loop, call plt.close(figure) after saving:

>>> for number, m in enumerate(matches.with_status("fp", "fn")):
...     figure = hires.plot.individual(m, scan, save=f"errors/{number:03d}.png")
...     plt.close(figure)

To draw only the outline of one annotation, without an image, use annotation. With obb=True it adds the minimum rotated rectangle from which body length and width are measured, and with bbox=True the axis-aligned bounding box:

>>> ax = hires.plot.annotation(
...     gt[0], image_size=gt.image_size, obb=True, bbox=True, save="plot_annotation.png"
... )

docs.title: Confusion matrix
docs.text:
>>> matrix = hires.metrics.confusion_matrix(gt, pred, class_names=names)
>>> matrix
pred        pulex  galeata  background
gt
pulex           2        0           0
galeata         1        1           1
background      0        1           0
>>> ax = hires.plot.confusion_matrix(matrix, save="plot_confusion.png")

Each row is normalized to sum to one, so the diagonal reads as recall per class. Pass normalize=False for raw counts.

docs.title: Precision-recall curves
docs.text:
>>> curve = hires.metrics.precision_recall_curve(gt, pred)
>>> ax = hires.plot.precision_recall(curve, save="plot_pr.png")

The marker shows the point with the best F1. To compare several curves, pass a dict of {label: curve}, for example one curve per class or one per model:

>>> curves = {
...     label: hires.metrics.precision_recall_curve(gt, pred, class_id=class_id)
...     for class_id, label in names.items()
... }
>>> ax = hires.plot.precision_recall(curves)

docs.title: Training curves
docs.text:
training_curves plots the training and validation losses from the results.csv that Ultralytics writes during training. With patience, a vertical line marks the best epoch, assuming training was ended by early stopping.

>>> figure = hires.plot.training_curves(  # doctest: +SKIP
...     "runs/segment/train/results.csv", patience=50
... )

docs.title: Composing figures
docs.text:
Chart functions accept ax=, so they fit into any Matplotlib layout:

>>> figure, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
>>> _ = hires.plot.confusion_matrix(matrix, ax=left, title="Confusion")
>>> _ = hires.plot.precision_recall(curve, ax=right, title="Precision-recall")
>>> figure.savefig("plot_composed.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")

docs.title: Working without a display
docs.text:
On a server or in a batch job, select a non-interactive Matplotlib backend before the first plot:

>>> import matplotlib
>>> matplotlib.use("Agg")

The hires command needs no such setup.

docs.title: Tiled segmentation
docs.text:
High-resolution scans routinely exceed 10,000 × 10,000 pixels. Passing such an image to a segmentation network in one piece is impossible on ordinary hardware, and downscaling it destroys the small objects one wants to measure. HiReS therefore processes the image tile by tile at full resolution and reassembles the result.

This page describes the algorithm and how to choose its parameters. The entry points are

Function Use it to hires.segment Segment one image in one call hires.Segmenter Segment many images with one loaded model hires.run_pipeline Segment files and write all outputs to disk

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
1. Tile. Cut the image into overlapping tiles.
  2. Predict. Run the model on every tile.
  3. Filter edges. Discard detections that touch a tile border.
  4. Merge. Transform the remaining polygons to full-image coordinates.
  5. Deduplicate. Remove duplicates from overlapping tiles with polygon non-maximum suppression (NMS).

The result is a Collection in full-image normalized coordinates, ordered by decreasing confidence.

docs.title: 1. Tiling
docs.text:
Tiles of size \(T\) are placed every \(T - o\) pixels along each axis, where \(o\) is the overlap, starting at the origin and continuing until the image is covered. An axis of length \(L > T\) therefore receives

\[ n = 1 + \left\lceil \frac{L - T}{T - o} \right\rceil \]

tiles, and an axis with \(L \le T\) exactly one. A tile is identified by the pixel coordinates \((x_0, y_0)\) of its top-left corner.

>>> import hires
>>> hires.tiling.tile_grid((2500, 900), tile_size=1024, overlap=150)
[(0, 0), (874, 0), (1748, 0)]

The last tile along an axis usually extends past the image border. The part outside the image is filled with zeros (black), so that every tile has the same size.

docs.title: 2. Prediction
docs.text: Tiles are passed to the model in batches of batch_size. Each tile is resized by the model to inference_size (the Ultralytics imgsz), and detections below confidence are dropped by the model itself. Each detection becomes an Annotation whose polygon is normalized to the tile.

docs.title: 3. Edge filtering
docs.text:
An object that crosses a tile border is seen only partially by that tile, and the model returns a truncated polygon for it. Measuring such a fragment would be wrong. HiReS discards every detection that is not fully contained in the tile shrunk by a margin \(m\) on every side:

\[ \text{keep} \iff \text{polygon} \subseteq [m,\, 1 - m] \times [m,\, 1 - m] \]

in tile-normalized coordinates, with \(m\) = edge_margin (default 0.01, i.e. about 10 px of a 1024 px tile). This is what Annotation.within_frame tests.

Discarding is safe because of the overlap: an object dropped from one tile lies fully inside the neighbouring tile, provided it is small enough (see Choosing the overlap).

docs.title: 4. Merging
docs.text:
A point \((x, y)\) normalized to a tile of size \((T_w, T_h)\) with corner \((x_0, y_0)\) maps to the full image of size \((W, H)\) as

\[ x' = \frac{x \, T_w + x_0}{W}, \qquad y' = \frac{y \, T_h + y_0}{H}. \]

After merging, the edge filter is applied once more, now to the full image, which removes objects cut by the border of the scan itself and detections in the zero-padded area.

The margin is relative

edge_margin is a fraction of the tile in step 3 and a fraction of the full image here. With the default of 0.01, objects within 1 % of the image width or height of the scan border are excluded. Set edge_margin=0 to keep everything, at the price of keeping fragments.

docs.title: 5. Non-maximum suppression
docs.text:
An object inside the overlap region is detected, in full, by two or more tiles. These duplicates are removed by Collection.nms:

  1. Sort the annotations by decreasing confidence; ties are broken in favour of the larger polygon.
  2. Take the first remaining annotation and keep it.
  3. Remove every remaining annotation whose polygon IoU with it exceeds nms_iou.
  4. Repeat from 2.

The intersection-over-union is computed on the polygons, not on their bounding boxes,

\[ \operatorname{IoU}(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}, \]

and candidate pairs are found with a spatial index (an STR-tree), so the cost grows with the number of overlapping pairs rather than with the square of the number of detections.

In the pipeline NMS is class-agnostic: two detections of the same object with different classes count as duplicates, and the more confident one wins.

docs.title: Choosing the overlap
docs.text:
Along one axis, consecutive tiles keep the detections inside windows that overlap by \(o - 2mT\) pixels. An object whose extent along that axis is smaller than this is therefore always fully inside at least one tile:

\[ d_{\max} < o - 2\,m\,T \]

With the defaults (\(o = 150\), \(m = 0.01\), \(T = 1024\)) objects up to about 130 px are guaranteed to be captured. Larger objects that happen to straddle a tile border are lost.

Rule of thumb

Set overlap to slightly more than the largest object you expect, in pixels. If large objects go missing in a regular grid pattern, the overlap is too small.

A larger overlap means more tiles and proportionally more inference time.

docs.title: Tile size and inference size
docs.text: tile_size is the size of the cut-out in the original image; inference_size is the size the model sees. Keep them equal to the tile size the model was trained on, so that objects appear at the scale the model learned. Setting tile_size larger than inference_size downsamples each tile: faster, but small objects lose detail.

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: A lower confidence finds more objects and more false positives. If you have ground truth, choose the threshold from the precision-recall curve rather than by eye; see Evaluation. To do so, run the model once with a low threshold and filter afterwards with filter_confidence.

docs.title: NMS threshold
docs.text: nms_iou (default 0.7) must be low enough to merge two detections of the same object from different tiles, which typically overlap almost perfectly, and high enough not to remove a genuinely different object that overlaps its neighbour. Lower it if you see doubled outlines; raise it if touching individuals disappear.

docs.text: Parameter Default Raise it when Lower it when tile_size 1024 — Out of memory during inference overlap 150 Large objects are missed at tile borders Runs are too slow confidence 0.5 Too many false positives Objects are missed inference_size 1024 Small objects are missed Out of memory, or too slow edge_margin 0.01 Truncated fragments survive Objects near borders are missed nms_iou 0.7 Touching objects are suppressed Duplicates survive batch_size 8 A GPU is under-used Out of memory

docs.title: Reusing a model
docs.text:
hires.segment loads the model on every call. For more than one image, create a Segmenter once:

segmenter = hires.Segmenter("DaphnAI.pt", overlap=300, device="0")

for path in hires.io.find_images("scans/"):
    collection = segmenter.segment(path)
    collection.to_txt(f"results/{path.stem}.txt")

segmenter.class_names returns the {class_id: label} mapping stored in the model, and segmenter.parameters() the settings as a plain dict.

docs.title: Arrays as input
docs.text:
segment also accepts an 8-bit BGR array of shape (height, width, 3):

pixels = hires.io.read_image("scan.tif")
collection = segmenter.segment(pixels, name="scan")

docs.title: Using another model
docs.text:
The model argument may be an already loaded object instead of a path. Any object works that provides

  • predict(tiles, conf=..., imgsz=..., device=..., verbose=False), returning one result per tile with masks.xyn (tile-normalized polygons), boxes.cls and boxes.conf, and
  • optionally names, a list or dict of class labels.

This is the interface of ultralytics.YOLO. Passing an object does not require the yolo extra.

docs.title: A worked example without a neural network
docs.text:
The interface above is small enough to write a toy "model" by hand, which makes the whole pipeline runnable in a few lines and shows what the parameters do. This one outlines every bright blob in a tile:

>>> from types import SimpleNamespace
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import cv2
>>> class BlobModel:
...     names = {0: "blob"}
...     def predict(self, tiles, conf, imgsz, device, verbose):
...         results = []
...         for tile in tiles:
...             height, width = tile.shape[:2]
...             mask = (tile[..., 0] > 128).astype(np.uint8)
...             contours, _ = cv2.findContours(
...                 mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE
...             )
...             polygons = [c.reshape(-1, 2) / (width, height) for c in contours]
...             boxes = SimpleNamespace(
...                 cls=np.zeros(len(polygons)), conf=np.full(len(polygons), 0.9)
...             )
...             masks = SimpleNamespace(xyn=polygons) if polygons else None
...             results.append(SimpleNamespace(masks=masks, boxes=boxes))
...         return results

The scan is a black 600 × 400 px image with three white squares of 40 px:

>>> scan = np.zeros((400, 600, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
>>> for x, y in [(50, 50), (240, 100), (450, 300)]:
...     scan[y : y + 40, x : x + 40] = 255

With 256 px tiles and an overlap of 64 px, the image is covered by six tiles, and all three squares are found exactly once:

>>> import hires
>>> hires.tiling.tile_grid((600, 400), tile_size=256, overlap=64)
[(0, 0), (0, 192), (192, 0), (192, 192), (384, 0), (384, 192)]
>>> found = hires.segment(scan, BlobModel(), tile_size=256, overlap=64)
>>> found
Collection(name=None, n=3, image_size=(600, 400))
>>> sorted(tuple(round(v) for v in a.to_pixels((600, 400)).bounds) for a in found)
[(50, 50, 89, 89), (240, 100, 279, 139), (450, 300, 489, 339)]

The second square spans x = 240…280 and therefore crosses the right border of the first tile (x = 256). That tile sees only a fragment and discards it; the neighbouring tile, which starts at x = 192, sees the square in full.

Now remove the overlap. The tile border at x = 256 still cuts the square, but no other tile contains it completely, and it is lost:

>>> len(hires.segment(scan, BlobModel(), tile_size=256, overlap=0))
2

Switching the edge filter off instead keeps the square, but as two separate fragments, which are the two small areas below:

>>> halves = hires.segment(scan, BlobModel(), tile_size=256, overlap=0, edge_margin=0)
>>> len(halves)
4
>>> sorted(int(a.to_pixels((600, 400)).area) for a in halves)
[585, 897, 1520, 1521]

Neither is what you want, which is why the overlap must exceed the size of the largest object.

A Segmenter holds the model and the settings, and is the object to reuse across images:

>>> segmenter = hires.Segmenter(BlobModel(), tile_size=256, overlap=64)
>>> segmenter.class_names
{0: 'blob'}
>>> segmenter.parameters()["overlap"], segmenter.parameters()["nms_iou"]
(64, 0.7)
>>> segmenter.segment(scan, name="again")
Collection(name='again', n=3, image_size=(600, 400))

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: The image is decoded completely into memory as an 8-bit, three-channel array, which takes \(3\,W H\) bytes (about 300 MB for a 10,000 × 10,000 px scan). Tiles are views into that array, so tiling itself costs almost nothing. Inference memory is governed by inference_size and batch_size, not by the size of the scan.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
To see what happens at each stage, pass debug_dir to Segmenter.segment (or debug=True to run_pipeline, or --debug on the command line):

segmenter.segment("scan.tif", debug_dir="debug/")
Path Content tiles/{name}_{x}_{y}.png Every tile tile_labels/{name}_{x}_{y}.txt Raw predictions of the tile, before edge filtering tile_overlays/{name}_{x}_{y}.png Raw predictions drawn on the tile {name}_merged.txt Edge-filtered detections in full-image coordinates, before NMS

Compare a tile overlay with the final result to tell whether an object was missed by the model, removed by the edge filter, or suppressed by NMS.

docs.title: Tiling training data
docs.text:
A model that is applied to tiles should be trained on tiles. This page shows how to cut annotated full-resolution images into a training set with the same geometry the segmentation pipeline uses at inference. The functions live in hires.tiling.

You do not need this page to run a model: hires.segment tiles and merges internally.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> import cv2
>>> from shapely.geometry import box
>>> import hires

docs.title: The tile grid
docs.text:
Tiles are placed every tile_size - overlap pixels, starting at the top-left corner, until the image is covered. Each tile is identified by the pixel coordinates (x, y) of its top-left corner in the full image. tile_grid returns these corners for an image of a given (width, height):

>>> hires.tiling.tile_grid((2500, 900), tile_size=1024, overlap=150)
[(0, 0), (874, 0), (1748, 0)]
>>> hires.tiling.tile_grid((300, 200), tile_size=128, overlap=28)
[(0, 0), (0, 100), (100, 0), (100, 100), (200, 0), (200, 100)]

The second grid, three columns by two rows of 128 px tiles placed every 100 px, is used in the rest of this page. Its last column and row extend past the image; the part outside is filled with zeros, so all tiles have the same size.

docs.title: Tiling images
docs.text:
iter_tiles yields the tiles of an image array:

>>> image = np.full((200, 300, 3), 200, dtype=np.uint8)
>>> for tile in hires.tiling.iter_tiles(image, tile_size=128, overlap=28):
...     print(tile.x, tile.y, tile.pixels.shape)
0 0 (128, 128, 3)
0 100 (128, 128, 3)
100 0 (128, 128, 3)
100 100 (128, 128, 3)
200 0 (128, 128, 3)
200 100 (128, 128, 3)

tile_image does the same for an image file and writes one PNG per tile, named {stem}_{x}_{y}.png. Bit depth and channels are preserved. The command-line equivalent is hires chunk.

>>> _ = cv2.imwrite("scan.png", image)
>>> paths = hires.tiling.tile_image("scan.png", "tiles/images", tile_size=128, overlap=28)
>>> [path.name for path in paths]
['scan_0_0.png', 'scan_0_100.png', 'scan_100_0.png', 'scan_100_100.png', 'scan_200_0.png', 'scan_200_100.png']

The position of a tile is recoverable from its file name:

>>> hires.tiling.parse_tile_name("scan_200_100.png")
('scan', 200, 100)

docs.title: Tiling annotations
docs.text:
tile_annotations is the counterpart for labels. Take a collection with two objects: a small one near the top-left corner, and a larger one in the middle of the image.

>>> collection = hires.Collection(
...     [
...         hires.Annotation(0, box(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25)),   # 30 x 30 px
...         hires.Annotation(1, box(0.37, 0.30, 0.60, 0.55)),   # 69 x 50 px
...     ],
...     name="scan",
...     image_size=(300, 200),
... )
>>> tiles = hires.tiling.tile_annotations(collection, tile_size=128, overlap=28)
>>> for position, tile in tiles.items():
...     print(position, tile)
(0, 0) Collection(name='scan_0_0', n=2, image_size=(128, 128))
(0, 100) Collection(name='scan_0_100', n=1, image_size=(128, 128))
(100, 0) Collection(name='scan_100_0', n=1, image_size=(128, 128))
(100, 100) Collection(name='scan_100_100', n=1, image_size=(128, 128))
(200, 0) Collection(name='scan_200_0', n=0, image_size=(128, 128))
(200, 100) Collection(name='scan_200_100', n=0, image_size=(128, 128))

The result maps every tile position to a Collection named {name}_{x}_{y}, the same stem as the tile image, with polygons normalized to the tile. Empty tiles are included.

The collection needs an image_size; read labels together with their image to get one (hires.read_txt(path, image=...)).

docs.title: Objects on a tile border
docs.text:
An annotation is assigned to every tile its bounding box overlaps and is not clipped. The second object lies across the borders of several tiles. In tile (0, 0) it sticks out on the right, so its coordinates exceed 1; tile (100, 0) contains it completely:

>>> [round(v, 2) for v in tiles[(0, 0)][1].bounds]
[0.87, 0.47, 1.41, 0.86]
>>> [round(v, 2) for v in tiles[(100, 0)][0].bounds]
[0.09, 0.47, 0.62, 0.86]

For training, drop these partial objects with within_frame, which is true for annotations that lie completely inside their tile:

>>> complete = {
...     position: tile.filter(lambda a: a.within_frame())
...     for position, tile in tiles.items()
... }
>>> for position, tile in complete.items():
...     print(position, len(tile))
(0, 0) 1
(0, 100) 0
(100, 0) 1
(100, 100) 0
(200, 0) 0
(200, 100) 0

Each object is now complete in at least one tile. This is the right choice for two reasons. Ultralytics rejects label files with coordinates outside [0, 1]. And it mirrors inference, where detections touching a tile border are discarded because the neighbouring tile sees the object in full (see Edge filtering).

The overlap must exceed the largest object

The second object is 69 × 50 px and the overlap only 28 px. It survived because it happens to fit inside tile (100, 0). An object is guaranteed to be complete in some tile only if the overlap is at least as large as the object. With too small an overlap, large objects silently vanish from the training set.

docs.title: Building a training set
docs.text:
Putting it together for a directory of scans and their label files:

>>> album = hires.read_album("labels/", image_dir="scans/")  # doctest: +SKIP
>>> tiled = []  # doctest: +SKIP
>>> for collection in album:  # doctest: +SKIP
...     hires.tiling.tile_image(collection.image_path, "dataset/images/")
...     tiles = hires.tiling.tile_annotations(collection)
...     tiled.extend(t.filter(lambda a: a.within_frame()) for t in tiles.values())
>>> dataset = hires.Album(tiled, name="dataset")  # doctest: +SKIP
>>> dataset.to_txt("dataset/labels/", confidence=False)  # doctest: +SKIP

confidence=False writes plain YOLO labels without a trailing confidence column, as training expects. With the example of this page:

>>> dataset = hires.Album(complete.values(), name="dataset")
>>> dataset
Album(name='dataset', collections=6, annotations=2)
>>> written = dataset.to_txt("tiles/labels", confidence=False)
>>> sorted(path.name for path in written)
['scan_0_0.txt', 'scan_0_100.txt', 'scan_100_0.txt', 'scan_100_100.txt', 'scan_200_0.txt', 'scan_200_100.txt']

Scans of sparse samples produce many empty tiles. To thin out tiles that contain only the dominant class, or nothing, balance the album before writing it; see Balancing a dataset.

Split by scan, not by tile

Overlapping tiles of one scan share pixels. Splitting them at random into training and validation sets leaks validation data into training and inflates the validation metrics. Assign whole scans to one set.

docs.title: Merging tiles back
docs.text:
merge_tiles is the inverse coordinate transform. It takes {(x, y): annotations} and returns one collection in full-image coordinates:

>>> merged = hires.tiling.merge_tiles(
...     complete, tile_size=128, image_size=(300, 200), name="scan"
... )
>>> merged
Collection(name='scan', n=2, image_size=(300, 200))
>>> [tuple(round(v, 2) for v in a.bounds) for a in merged]
[(0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.25), (0.37, 0.3, 0.6, 0.55)]

Both objects are back at their original positions. An object that is complete in several overlapping tiles appears once per tile in the merged result. For predictions, remove such duplicates with Collection.nms; this is what the segmentation pipeline does.

To merge tile label files from disk, recover the positions from the file names:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from_disk = {}
>>> for path in sorted(Path("tiles/labels").glob("scan_*.txt")):
...     _, x, y = hires.tiling.parse_tile_name(path)
...     from_disk[(x, y)] = hires.read_txt(path)
>>> hires.tiling.merge_tiles(from_disk, tile_size=128, image_size=(300, 200))
Collection(name=None, n=2, image_size=(300, 200))
